_readme: Electricity prices for the Europe AC cost pages. rate is the price per kWh in local currency that running an air conditioner adds to a bill (see rateNote for exactly what it is). Each country has its own source and date: update rate, asOf and source together, then bump 'updated'. hours per city are our estimate of full-load cooling hours a year for a split AC (the EU energy label assumes 350 for an average European climate). usdPerEur and gbpPerEur are for the U.S./UK comparisons only.

countries.name: Spain
countries.rateNote: average household price, all taxes and fixed charges included
countries.source: Eurostat, electricity prices for household consumers (nrg_pc_204), 2,500–4,999 kWh a year, all taxes and levies
tariff: Most Spanish homes are on a time-of-use tariff (2.0TD). On weekdays, 10:00–14:00 and 18:00–22:00 are the peak (punta) hours, 08:00–10:00, 14:00–18:00 and 22:00–24:00 are mid (llano), and nights and weekends are off-peak (valle). Afternoon and evening AC falls in the peak and mid periods, so pre-cooling in the morning and setting the thermostat a little higher at peak saves money.

On the regulated PVPC tariff the energy price changes every hour with the wholesale market, so a hot week with high demand can cost more than the average shown here. The figure here is Eurostat's average, which also spreads fixed power charges over every kWh.

countries.name: France
countries.rateNote: price per kWh on EDF's regulated Tarif Bleu (Base option), tax included
countries.source: EDF Tarif Bleu regulated tariff (TRVE), Base option, price per kWh including tax, from August 1, 2026
tariff: The Tarif Bleu also has a fixed monthly subscription (about €15.86 a month at 6 kVA), which doesn't change with how much you run the AC. On the off-peak option (heures pleines / heures creuses), peak kWh cost €0.2142 and off-peak €0.1589, so a timer that pre-cools during off-peak hours helps.
On the Tempo option, the expensive red days only fall between November and March, so summer cooling runs on cheaper blue and white days.

countries.name: Portugal
countries.rateNote: price per kWh on the regulated simple tariff (6.9 kVA) with 23% VAT, which applies to use above 200 kWh a month
countries.source: Regulated tariff (SU Eletricidade, ERSE), simple tariff at 6.9 kVA: €0.1711/kWh before VAT (Selectra, updated October 13, 2026), plus 23% VAT
tariff: VAT is what makes AC more expensive than it looks. For contracted power up to 6.9 kVA, the first 200 kWh in each 30-day period are taxed at 6% (300 kWh for large families), and everything above at 23%. Air conditioning usually pushes a summer bill past that line, so the extra kWh it uses pay the full 23%.

On the two-period tariff (bi-horário), off-peak (vazio) kWh cost €0.1143 and peak (fora de vazio) €0.2045 before VAT, so running the AC harder in the cheaper hours helps. Most households are on the free market, where prices are usually close to the regulated tariff.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.rateNote: Ofgem price cap unit rate (Direct Debit, GB average, no VAT)
countries.source: Ofgem energy price cap, electricity unit rate, Direct Debit, GB average, October 1 to December 31, 2026
tariff: Under the price cap you also pay a daily standing charge of 54.83p, but that's fixed: running the AC only adds the unit rate. The price cap changes every three months, and fixed-price deals can be cheaper or dearer. The government has removed VAT from electricity bills from October 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027, and the cap figures already reflect that.

Few UK homes have air conditioning, so the realistic choice in a heatwave is usually a portable unit or a single wall-mounted split. Time-of-use tariffs with cheap overnight rates don't help much, because cooling is needed in the afternoon and evening.
